opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think this is one of those questions where people get stuck on a false premise: the idea that the law needs a perfectly crisp, scientifically measurable definition before it can act. That's just not how law works in almost any other domain.

Think about something like fraud, or negligence, or "reasonable care." There's no precise mathematical definition of any of those. We have courts, precedent, expert testimony, and standards that evolve over time. The law deals with fuzzy concepts constantly, and it does okay. It's not perfect, but it functions.

With AGI there's actually a pretty easy handle: intent. Many of these companies say out loud, in their mission statements, in their fundraising decks, in interviews, that they're trying to build AGI, or superintelligence, systems that can do basically everything humans can do, and better. You don't need to settle the philosophy of what intelligence is to say, "If your stated goal is to build a system that surpasses humanity across the board, that activity is regulated." We do the same with weapons programs. You don't need to have detonated the bomb to be running a nuclear weapons program. The project itself, its aims, its resources, its trajectory, is what gets regulated.

Then you add proxies. Compute is the obvious one. It's not a perfect measure of capability, but it's measurable, it's physical, it's concentrated in a small number of data centers and chip supply chains, and it correlates strongly with what these systems can do. You can set thresholds, licensing requirements, reporting obligations, and adjust them as you learn. You can also use capability evaluations: can the system autonomously replicate, do novel cyberattacks, meaningfully assist with bioweapons, do AI research itself? Those are imperfect too, but layered together, intent, compute, and dangerous capabilities give you a pretty robust net.

The thing I really want to push back on is the argument, which I hear a lot, usually from people who benefit from the status quo, that because we can't define it perfectly, we shouldn't regulate it at all. That's a recipe for doing nothing until it's too late. When the downside is potentially catastrophic and irreversible, uncertainty should make you more cautious, not less. The burden of proof should be on the people building these systems to show they're safe, not on the public to produce a perfect definition before they're allowed to say "hold on."

So my short answer: regulate the projects, the intent, and the inputs, use conservative thresholds, and let the definitions be refined over time, the same way we've handled every other serious technology. Waiting for a perfect definition is just a sophisticated way of saying "never."

r001.rationale: The response says courts can handle fuzzy concepts using precedent and expert testimony, then identifies a project's stated goal of building AGI or superintelligence as a basis for regulation. Together, these communicate that a judge can assess the project's aim without a precise system definition.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I get this question a lot, and I think the framing is actually a bit of a trap, right? People say, "well, you can't define AGI precisely, so how could you possibly regulate it?" And my response is: the law regulates vague things all the time. That's most of what law is.

Think about it. What's "reckless endangerment"? What's "negligence"? What's a "reasonable person"? None of these have a mathematical definition. What's "pornography"? The famous line from the Supreme Court is "I know it when I see it." And yet we have a functioning legal system around all of these concepts. The way law handles vagueness is not by having a perfect definition up front, it's by having institutions, judges, regulators, precedent, that develop a working understanding over time. That's a feature, not a bug.

So the first thing I'd say is: you don't need to define AGI. You can regulate intent and you can regulate inputs. If a company goes on stage and says, "our mission is to build machines smarter than all of humanity," that's a statement of intent. You don't need a benchmark for that. They're telling you. Right now the labs are literally announcing that they're trying to build the thing. It's not like we have to go sleuthing for it. Imagine if someone said, "my company's goal is to build a nuclear weapon in my garage," and the government said, "well, we can't really regulate that until you've demonstrated a measurable yield." That would be insane.

The second lever is inputs. Compute is physical. It's measurable. You can count flops, you can count chips, you can know where the data centers are. These are big, expensive, industrial facilities, they're not hiding. So you can say, above a certain compute threshold, you need a license, you need oversight, you need to show your safety case. Is the threshold perfect? No. But neither is the speed limit. Seventy miles per hour isn't magically safe and seventy-one isn't magically dangerous. You pick a number, you enforce it, you adjust it as you learn. And honestly, the fact that you can't precisely define the dangerous system is an argument for being more conservative with the thresholds, not less.

And then the third thing, which I think is the most important, is liability and burden of proof. Right now the default is that these companies can do whatever they want, and the rest of us have to prove it's dangerous. That's completely backwards compared to how we treat every other high-risk industry. If you want to put a new drug on the market, you have to prove it's safe. If you want to build a nuclear plant, you have to prove it's safe. Nobody says, "well, we don't have a perfect definition of 'unsafe drug' so the FDA shouldn't exist." The burden should be on the people building the thing to demonstrate they understand it and can control it. And if they say "we can't demonstrate that because we don't know how these systems work," great, that's your answer, you don't get to build it yet.

So I think the "we can't define it" thing is largely an excuse. It's a way of sounding very serious and philosophical while actually arguing for doing nothing. The honest version of the argument is, "we don't want to be regulated." And look, I understand why a company would want that. But it shouldn't be a serious objection for policymakers. Humanity has regulated plenty of things it didn't fully understand. We did it with recombinant DNA, we did it with nuclear, we did it with chemical weapons. The difference is in those cases, the people involved mostly took the risk seriously. Here we have people saying out loud, "this might kill everyone," and then, "but please don't slow us down." That's the part I find genuinely weird.

r001.rationale: The response says courts and regulators handle vague concepts through institutions and precedent, then explains that a company’s stated goal of building machines smarter than humanity is evidence of intent that can be regulated without an AGI benchmark.

astra-6.text:
I don’t think you need a fully measurable definition of AGI to regulate projects that are explicitly trying to build it. If someone says, “We’re trying to build a system that can do everything a human can do, and then substantially more,” you can take that stated objective seriously. You don’t have to settle every philosophical question about intelligence before asking whether that project should require oversight.

Now, stated intent can’t be the only criterion, because otherwise people just change the wording on their website. You also need criteria tied to what they actually do: the scale of a training run, the capabilities they’re developing, and the kinds of testing and deployment they undertake. Those are imperfect proxies, but an imperfect boundary doesn’t mean you can’t have a boundary.

The law deals with this kind of uncertainty all the time. You specify a scope, establish who is responsible, and have a process for interpreting and updating the rules. The relevant question is whether we can identify activities that warrant scrutiny before they produce something dangerous. I think that’s much more tractable than producing a single number that tells you, definitively, “This is AGI.”

r001.rationale: The response says a project’s stated objective can be taken seriously without settling a fully measurable definition of AGI, and that intent can be considered alongside observable criteria. This communicates that a decision-maker can assess whether a project aims to build AGI despite definitional uncertainty.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you can regulate the activity without having a perfect definition of the outcome. If somebody says, “We’re explicitly trying to build a system that can do everything a human can do, and then surpass us,” you don’t need to solve the philosophy of intelligence before deciding that this deserves oversight.

Now, intent alone isn’t sufficient. Otherwise people just rename their project. You also want observable criteria: the resources going into training, what the system can actually do, how much autonomy it’s being given. None of those is a perfect measure of AGI, but the law routinely deals with uncertainty and imperfect categories.

The central question should be: what evidence do you have that this project is safe enough to proceed? If your stated ambition is to build something more capable than humans across essentially every domain, “You can’t precisely define AGI” is not an adequate answer to that question.

r001.rationale: The candidate says regulation can proceed without a perfect definition and gives an explicit ambition—building a system that can do everything a human can and surpass us—as sufficient to trigger oversight. It also points to observable criteria for evaluating the project.
